questions.q: Define deductive reasoning and give one example from daily life that is not from the textbook.
questions.a: Deductive reasoning is reasoning from a general principle or premise to a specific conclusion; if the premises are true and the logic is valid, the conclusion must be true. Example: "All students in Class 11 must submit the project by Friday. Rahul is a Class 11 student. Therefore, Rahul must submit the project by Friday." A wrong answer (e.g., defining it as reasoning from specific to general) reveals confusion with inductive reasoning.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the conclusion "All crows are black because I have seen 100 black crows" is an inductive argument and not a deductive one.
questions.a: The argument is inductive because it generalizes from specific observations (100 black crows) to a universal claim (all crows are black); the conclusion is probable but not certain — a single non-black crow would falsify it. Deductive reasoning would require a premise like "All birds of species Corvus are black" to guarantee the conclusion. A wrong answer that calls this deductive shows misunderstanding of the direction of inference and the role of certainty.

questions.q: A student argues: "Every time I study with music, I get good marks. Therefore, listening to music causes good marks." Identify the type of reasoning and explain one flaw in this reasoning.
questions.a: This is inductive reasoning (specific instances → general causal claim). The flaw is confusing correlation with causation — other factors (e.g., study duration, prior knowledge) could explain the marks; the conclusion goes beyond the evidence. A wrong answer that labels it deductive or misses the correlation-causation error shows inability to apply reasoning types to real situations.

questions.q: Compare deductive and inductive reasoning on three dimensions: (a) direction of inference, (b) certainty of conclusion, (c) dependence on premise truth.
questions.a: (a) Deductive: general → specific; Inductive: specific → general. (b) Deductive: conclusion certain if premises true and valid; Inductive: conclusion probable, never certain. (c) Deductive: validity depends on logical structure, but soundness requires true premises; Inductive: strength depends on quality/quantity of evidence. A wrong answer that claims inductive conclusions can be certain or that deduction does not need true premises reveals incomplete analysis.

questions.q: Evaluate this argument: "All mammals have lungs. A whale is a mammal. Therefore, a whale has lungs." Is it valid? Is it sound? Justify.
questions.a: The argument is valid (structure: All A are B; C is A; therefore C is B) and sound because both premises are factually true. A wrong answer that says it is valid but not sound (or vice versa) without justification shows confusion between logical validity (form) and soundness (form + true premises).

questions.q: Create a short scenario (3-4 sentences) that illustrates a person using *both* deductive and inductive reasoning sequentially to solve a problem.
questions.a: Example: "Riya notices her phone battery drains quickly after installing a new app (inductive observation: specific instances → hypothesis: the app causes drain). She then recalls the general rule: 'Background apps consume battery' (deductive premise) and concludes: 'If I restrict this app's background activity, my battery will last longer' (deductive application)." A poor answer that uses only one type or sequences them illogically shows inability to synthesize both reasoning modes.
